newsitem.title: UK: CWS escapes bid but not profits problems.
newsitem.headline: CWS escapes bid but not profits problems.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) may be relieved to have escaped a hostile 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) bid but will need to boost profits and prove it can use its assets better to avoid further unwanted attention.
CWS on Friday was granted a permanent injunction barring entrepeneur Andrew Regan and his bidding vehicle Galileo from using confidential information about the group in any takeover offer.
Regan's plans were to convert the mutually-owned Co-op into a limited company and sell off some of its businesses.
The Co-op's activities span banking, insurance, travel agents, funeral parlours and food retailing.

Although the immediate threat of takeover has now receded, analysts say the Co-op clearly needs to look at ways of boosting the value of its assets in order to bolster itself against any future attacks.
CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth said at results earlier this month that his priority for action was mainstream retailing.
"He is targeting the organisation's 700 food and non-food stores to improve their performance. He wants them to operate as well as the best of CWS businesses," a statement from the company said.

Its food retailing operations have turnover of around 1.04 billion pounds and brought in profits of 37 million pounds, down 14 percent on the year after paying out three million in dividends to members.

The food services operations, which saw turnover slip four percent to 1.3 billion pounds, are intended to be non-profit making, a spokesman pointed out. "We intend this business only to cover costs," he said.

Melmoth's plans for the food retail operations include centralising operations of over 50 co-operative societies and a strategy of segmenting these into four retail formats -- superstores, supermarkets, convenience stores and village stores.
The Co-op runs around 650 food stores in total, with some 14 million square feet of retailing space, around the same selling area as Britain's leading supermarket group Tesco Plc.
But Tesco's annual sales, by contrast, are nearly 15 billion pounds and it made 750 million pounds of profit in the year to February 22, 1997.
Around 60-70 of the Co-op's food stores are supermarkets and the company said it would focus investment here as well as in convenience stores and technology.
During the Co-op's legal wrangles, it emerged that supermarket chain J. Sainsbury Plc had been in talks with Regan about buying some of the larger CWS properties.
But in a letter to the Co-op's lawyers, Sainsbury said it had returned all the information it had received and broke off talks a week ago.
Food retailing in Britain is highly competitive, with food price inflation currently virtually flat and supermarkets vying to offer customers loyalty cards and improved services.
Tesco, Sainsbury and Safeway all offer customer loyalty cards and are currently taking their first steps into banking, using the trust in their food brand to tempt financial customers.
In some ways, the Co-op's dividend was a precursor to loyalty cards. It currently offers customers five pence for every pound spent on own-brand goods.
It also has a banking arm, the Co-operative Bank, which turned in annual pretax profits of 45.5 million pounds earlier this month, an increase of 24 percent.
Although the Co-op Bank holds only three percent of the market it has successfully targeted higher earning customers with telephone banking and other innovations.
It is also known for its ethical and environmental stance and this image could be extended to food retail, observers suggested.

The CWS has said that it is differentiating itself from other supermarkets as the "responsible retailer" and has a free phone line for customers with queries on controversial topics such as genetically modified goods.
Perhaps the Co-op food retail business might find its "distinctive consumer niche" through promotion of its mutual and socially caring image.
William Morrison had pretax profits of 136 million pounds on turnover of 2.18 billion in year ending february 2. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
